a45.speaker: Cléophile Akindavyi, Director General, Burundi Ministry of Public Health and the Fight against AIDS (speaking on behalf of the Minister)
a45.speech: Thanked the United States, via USAID, for its continuous multifaceted support in public health and other sectors. Recalled that Mpore activity builds on two prior USAID-funded projects (Giriteka and GBV-Bridge activity). Stressed that "GBV remains a gateway to HIV/AIDS." Promised the Ministry of Health will provide full support for the project's implementation.

a45.speaker: Lisa Peterson, US Ambassador to Burundi
a45.speech: Stated that the Mpore activity project's overall objective is to improve and integrate gender-based violence (GBV) prevention into HIV and family-planning services and to strengthen the health system, at a cost of $6,350,000, covering Bujumbura Mairie, Bujumbura, Gitega, Rumonge and Makamba provinces.

a45.speaker: Spès Caritas Bishoboye, deputy legal representative of Swaa-Burundi
a45.speech: Thanked the US Embassy for entrusting her organization, via USAID, with implementing the Mpore activity project with two sub-partners. Commended the Government of Burundi for its multifaceted support. Called for the involvement of everyone — administration, police, justice, and GBV care structures — in the fight against GBV. Promised that Swaa-Burundi "will spare no effort" to achieve the project's objectives.

a45.speaker: Jean Bosco Uwimana, GBV sensitization worker (Giriteka project), Busoni commune
a45.speech: Testified that the predecessor Giriteka project bore fruit. Described helping a family with malnourished children get care, after the mother revealed she was a victim of sexual harassment by her husband; said he helped the couple access family-planning services, and concluded that the family now leads a normal life.

a45.speaker: Victor Segasago, Governor of Kirundo province
a45.speech: In his welcome address, welcomed the Mpore activity project, which includes his province in its area of operation, saying he expects many results and hopes it will contribute to the good health of the population so they can devote themselves to development work towards the 2040-2060 vision. Invited the administrative authorities to contribute to the implementation and success of the project.

a81.speaker: Dr. Jallah Barbu, Executive Director of Liberia's Office of War and Economic Crimes Court
a81.speech: Says he is honored to have the role and understands the weight of expectation he carries for the millions of Liberians still suffering the aftermath of the war.

a121.speaker: Ibrahim Traoré, President of Burkina Faso
a121.speech: In his inaugural statement, said Burkina Faso faced an emergency, citing crises in security, defence, healthcare, social action and infrastructure; he pledged to combat terrorism and adhere to the transition timetable agreed with the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS), which aimed to restore democratic rule by 1 July 2024.

a121.speaker: Ibrahim Traoré, President of Burkina Faso
a121.speech: Has rejected financial assistance from the International Monetary Fund and World Bank, insisting the country can develop without the West’s loans and conditionalities.

a121.speaker: Afrobarometer (survey)
a121.speech: Reports that almost two-thirds of Burkinabé believe the army should intervene when leaders abuse their power, and that 66 per cent accept military rule, up from 24 per cent in 2012.

a121.speaker: 2023/2024 Human Development Report
a121.speech: According to it, Burkina Faso is classified as having low human development and is ranked 185th out of 193 countries on the Human Development Index.

a121.speaker: Institute for Security Studies’ African Futures and Innovation team (research/study)
a121.speech: Recent research shows that Burkina Faso’s economy could grow at an average rate of 8 per cent from 2025 to 2043, which would translate into an additional GDP per capita of $1,120 above a business-as-usual forecast and reduce income poverty to only 2.6 per cent of the population, meaning an extra 2.4 million Burkinabés could be lifted out of poverty by 2043 ; the study identified governance reforms as critical to unlocking the country’s development potential, finding that good governance could raise GDP per capita by an extra $240 above a business-as-usual forecast, lifting 500,000 additional Burkinabé out of extreme poverty.

a121.speaker: UN Refugee Agency
a121.speech: Estimates that over two million people are internally displaced, and those needing humanitarian assistance increased by 35 per cent between 2022 and 2023.

a167.speaker: Ismail Haniyeh, Hamas leader
a167.speech: Stated that the killing of three of his sons and four grandchildren in an Israeli airstrike would not alter Hamas's stance in ongoing truce negotiations; speaking to Qatari broadcaster Al Jazeera, he suggested that the strike was an attempt to shift Hamas's negotiating stance.

a167.speaker: Israel (official confirmation)
a167.speech: Israel confirmed the killings of Haniyeh's three sons.

a167.speaker: Joe Biden, US President
a167.speech: Said Hamas "needs to move" on the latest truce proposal: "It's now up to Hamas, they need to move on the proposal that's been made".

a167.speaker: Joe Biden, US President
a167.speech: Labelled Netanyahu's handling of the war a "mistake" in an interview broadcast on Tuesday, before warning on Wednesday that Israel has not allowed enough aid into the territory: "I think what he's doing is a mistake," Biden told the US network Univision; he urged Netanyahu to "just call for a ceasefire, allow for the next six, eight weeks, total access to all food and medicine going into" Gaza.

a167.speaker: Joe Biden, US President
a167.speech: Promised "ironclad" support to Israel in response to Iran's threats: "As I told Prime Minister Netanyahu, our commitment to Israel's security against these threats from Iran and its proxies is ironclad."

a167.speaker: Hossam Badran, Hamas spokesperson in Doha
a167.speech: Told AFP: "Hamas is studying the offer presented... It has not responded yet."

a167.speaker: Witnesses
a167.speech: Witnesses said Israel carried out strikes early Thursday in the Gaza Strip, particularly in the south of the territory.

a167.speaker: Israeli figures (official)
a167.speech: According to Israeli figures, Hamas's 7 October attack against Israel resulted in the deaths of 1,170 people, mostly civilians.

a167.speaker: Israeli army
a167.speech: Says 34 of the 129 hostages remaining in Gaza are dead.

a167.speaker: Health ministry of the Hamas-run territory
a167.speech: According to the Hamas-run territory's health ministry, Israel's retaliatory offensive has killed at least 33,482 people in Gaza, mostly women and children.

a167.speaker: Pedro Sanchez, Spanish Prime Minister
a167.speech: Warned that what he called Israel's "disproportionate response" in Gaza risked "destabilising the Middle East, and as a consequence, the entire world".

a167.speaker: Benny Gantz, Israeli war cabinet member
a167.speech: Said that militarily, "Hamas is defeated" but pledged to continue fighting "what remains of it", including in the years to come; he also echoed Netanyahu's vows to enter the southern city of Rafah: "We will enter Rafah. We will return to Khan Yunis."

a167.speaker: Samantha Power, USAID Administrator (US Agency for International Development)
a167.speech: Said recent days had seen a "sea change" in aid deliveries, although she insisted Israel needs to do more.

a167.speaker: Yoav Gallant, Israeli Defence Minister
a167.speech: Said Israel would "flood Gaza with aid", using a new crossing point on its northern border, streamlined checks and two new routes organised with Jordan; he said they expected to hit 500 aid trucks entering Gaza a day, which would match the average level of aid and commercial trucks reaching the territory before the war.

a167.speaker: Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, Iran's supreme leader
a167.speech: Warned Israel on Wednesday that it "must be punished and will be punished" for a strike on the Iranian consulate in Damascus that Tehran has blamed on Israel.

a167.speaker: Israel Katz, Israeli Foreign Minister
a167.speech: Replied with a Persian-language post saying: "If Iran attacks from its territory, Israel will respond and attack Iran".

a167.speaker: Lufthansa (German airline)
a167.speech: Announced on Wednesday that it had suspended flights to and from Tehran, probably until Thursday, saying it was "due to the current situation in the Middle East".

a185.speaker: Madina Iltireh, Djibouti-Canadian former diplomat who served at Canada's embassy in Kuwait
a185.speech: Says she was forced to turn to the Federal Court after Global Affairs Canada repeatedly dismissed her complaints of discrimination and harassment, and that her three-year posting in Kuwait between 2018 and 2021 left her traumatized and isolated: "I was representing Canada, but Canada did not represent me" ; "I went through hell" ; "The place I was for three years was toxic, and it was suffocating. I developed anxiety, I lost memory, and I'm still trying to rebuild what I lost."

a185.speaker: Madina Iltireh, former Canadian diplomat
a185.speech: Says she received neither an apology nor compensation: "I need the department to show me change and to prove that what I went through will never happen again" ; "Hopefully, the ministry will change so the people coming after me don't have to go through what I did."

a185.speaker: Federal Court of Canada (ruling)
a185.speech: In 2024, the Federal Court ordered Global Affairs Canada (GAC) to reopen the investigation.

a185.speaker: Global Affairs Canada investigation report (obtained by Radio-Canada)
a185.speech: The subsequent report found four of the eight allegations to be founded, concluding that the ambassador "failed to ensure that Madina Iltireh worked in a healthy work environment" and had "encouraged and tolerated" bullying in the workplace. The report cited testimony suggesting that Iltireh faced sustained hostility from embassy staff, who criticized her tone, questioned her competence, and excluded her from meetings. It also found that her living conditions in Kuwait were substandard: a failing air conditioner, power outages, and delayed maintenance requests that went unaddressed for years.

a185.speaker: Nicholas Marcus Thompson, executive director of the Black Class Action Secretariat
a185.speech: Said Iltireh's experience mirrors dozens of cases from Black and racialized public servants across federal departments: "The system is dysfunctional. Workers are silenced, complaints are blocked, and while those who speak up suffer, the leadership advances." His organization is pressing Ottawa to create an independent investigative body to handle discrimination claims and implement overdue reforms to the Employment Equity Act.

a185.speaker: Tariq Gordon, career diplomat and co-founder of a peer support group within Global Affairs Canada
a185.speech: Said Iltireh's ordeal spotlights deep-rooted cultural problems within the foreign service: "She's not an isolated case. There are so many stories of people suffering quietly, afraid to jeopardize their careers by speaking up."

a185.speaker: Global Affairs Canada (written statement)
a185.speech: GAC, in a written statement, said it enforces a "zero-tolerance policy toward misconduct or wrongdoing" and that its internal investigators are trained to act "professionally and impartially." It added that the department is studying the creation of a standardized complaint intake model to improve transparency and recourse for staff.

a185.speaker: Anita Anand, Canadian Foreign Affairs Minister
a185.speech: Acknowledged the seriousness of the allegations, saying discrimination in any form is "unacceptable": "We need a public service where inclusivity and diversity are stronger because that makes our organizations and our country stronger. It's a priority for me as a minister and as a racialized woman."

a290.speaker: Residents and medics in northern Gaza
a290.speech: Said Israeli forces besieged hospitals and shelters for displaced people in the northern Gaza Strip on Monday as they stepped up their operations against Palestinian militants, and that troops rounded up men and ordered women to leave the Jabalia historic refugee camp ; said Israeli forces had tightened their siege on Jabalia by positioning tanks in nearby Beit Hanoun and Beit Lahiya towns and ordering residents to leave.

a290.speaker: Medics in Gaza
a290.speech: Said an Israeli airstrike on a house in Jabalia killed five people and wounded several others ; said Israeli strikes killed at least five people in Rafah in the southern Gaza Strip and four in two separate strikes in Gaza City.

a290.speaker: UNRWA (U.N. Palestinian refugee agency)
a290.speech: Said Israeli authorities were preventing humanitarian missions from reaching areas in the north of the Palestinian enclave with critical supplies, including medicine and food.

a290.speaker: Philippe Lazzarini, UNRWA head (post on X)
a290.speech: "People attempting to flee are getting killed, their bodies left on the street."

a290.speaker: Philippe Lazzarini, UNRWA head
a290.speech: Said injured people were lying without care in hospitals that had been hit ; "UNRWA remaining shelters are so overcrowded, some displaced people are now forced to live in the toilets."

a290.speaker: Medics at the Indonesian Hospital
a290.speech: Told Reuters that Israeli troops stormed a school and detained the men before setting it ablaze, and that the fire reached hospital generators and caused a power outage.

a290.speaker: Health officials in northern Gaza
a290.speech: Said they had refused orders by the Israeli army to evacuate the three hospitals in the area or leave the patients unattended, and said troops remained outside the hospital but did not enter.

a290.speaker: Medics at Kamal Adwan hospital
a290.speech: Reported heavy Israeli fire near the hospital at night.

a290.speaker: Unnamed nurse at the Indonesian Hospital
a290.speech: "The army is burning the schools next to the hospital, and no one can enter or leave the hospital."

a290.speaker: Palestinian health officials
a290.speech: Said at least 18 people had been killed in Jabalia and eight elsewhere in Gaza in Israeli strikes.

a290.speaker: Israeli military (statement)
a290.speech: Said it was operating against "terrorists and terrorist infrastructure" in the Jabalia area ; said troops had helped thousands of civilians to evacuate safely through organised routes, that Israel was in contact with the international community and Gaza's healthcare system to ensure hospital emergency services were operating, and that in the past day troops had dismantled militant infrastructure and tunnel shafts and killed fighters in the Jabalia area.

a290.speaker: Raed, a resident of Jabalia camp
a290.speech: "We are facing death by bombs, by thirst and hunger." ; "Jabalia is being wiped out and there is no witness to the crime, the world is blinding its eyes."

a290.speaker: Hadeel Obeid, supervisor nurse at the Indonesian hospital
a290.speech: Told Reuters they were running out of medical supplies, including sterile gauze and medications, that the water supply has been cut off and there was no food for the fourth consecutive day.

a290.speaker: United Nations
a290.speech: Said it had been unable to reach the three hospitals in northern Gaza.

a290.speaker: U.N. Human Rights Office
a290.speech: Accused Israeli forces of unlawful interference with humanitarian assistance and of issuing orders that were causing forced displacement, saying their conduct "may be causing the destruction of the Palestinian population in Gaza's northernmost governate through death and displacement".

a290.speaker: Israel (government)
a290.speech: Says it is getting large quantities of humanitarian supplies into Gaza with land deliveries and airdrops, and says it has facilitated the evacuation of patients from the Kamal Adwan Hospital.

a290.speaker: Palestinians
a290.speech: Say no aid entered northern Gaza areas where the operation is active.

a290.speaker: Israeli officials
a290.speech: Said evacuation orders were aimed at separating Hamas fighters from civilians and denied there was any systematic plan to clear out civilians; said forces operating in northern Gaza killed scores of Hamas gunmen and dismantled infrastructure.

a290.speaker: Hamas
a290.speech: Accused Israel of carrying out acts of "genocide and ethnic cleansing" to force people to leave northern Gaza.

a290.speaker: Hamas armed wing
a290.speech: Said fighters attacked forces there with anti-tank rockets and mortar fire, and detonated bombs against troops inside tanks and stationed in houses.

a290.speaker: Israeli tallies
a290.speech: According to Israeli tallies, the Oct. 7 cross-border attack on Israeli communities killed around 1,200 people, with about 253 more taken back to Gaza as hostages.

a290.speaker: Gaza health authorities
a290.speech: Say Israel's subsequent war has killed more than 42,500 Palestinians, with another 10,000 uncounted dead thought to lie under the rubble.

a536.speaker: Nyesom Wike, FCT Minister (represented by Grace Adayilo, Head of Service, FCTA)
a536.speech: Has called on the FCT and its neighbouring states to adopt modern crime-fighting techniques to combat cross-border crimes ; said such crimes are already threatening Abuja and its neighbours ; noted that in a rapidly evolving world, criminals have adapted and exploited technological advancements to further their illicit activities ; highlighted the need for a dynamic approach, including synergy and joint operations, to overcome the exploits of these individuals.

a536.speaker: Ajao Adewale, FCT Commissioner of Police
a536.speech: Said the G-7 security summit was conceived with the vision of tackling cross-border crimes in all their manifestations, including the challenges of kidnapping, banditry, car snatching, and human trafficking within the FCT and its contiguous states.

a566.speaker: European Union (press statement)
a566.speech: In a press statement on Thursday, the Western bloc said the fund will be mobilized in the next three years as an additional contribution to the 2021-2027 cooperation programme in the country, and stated that the grant is an expression of its long-term commitment to South Sudan and its people; it will support three priority sectors including green and resilient economy, human development and good governance as well as peace and rule of law to achieve a just society.

a566.speaker: European Union (press statement)
a566.speech: While expressing regrets over the transitional period extension, the bloc says the increased development assistance is not intended to fund the implementation of the extended government tenure; it reaffirms commitment to the South Sudan partnership in many areas including agriculture, health, education and governance by supporting the country’s transition to democracy.

a566.speaker: European Union (press statement)
a566.speech: Calls on the government to substantially increase its funding for the peace agreement implementation and provide social services to its own population, including the payment of salaries.

a566.speaker: European Union (press statement)
a566.speech: Said it has supported South Sudan since its independence in 2011, leveraging policy and political advocacy on key priorities, in close coordination with its Member States and the international community.

a751.speaker: Dr. Cassiel Ato Forson, Ghana's Finance Minister
a751.speech: Described the project as "transformational," noting that travel speeds are expected to more than triple, while journey times and freight delays will be drastically reduced.

a751.speaker: Dr. Cassiel Ato Forson, Ghana's Finance Minister
a751.speech: Expressed government's appreciation to JICA for its continued partnership with Ghana, stressing that the project forms part of a broader infrastructure agenda to modernize Kumasi's road network; and assured that these investments, when completed, will significantly boost connectivity, enhance trade, and contribute to economic growth in both Kumasi and the wider Ashanti Region.

a905.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a905.speech: Proclaimed on Tuesday that the “American dream is unstoppable” in his first address to Congress since a whirlwind return to power; said he was “just getting started” on his radical plans to reshape the country ; “We have accomplished more in 43 days than most administrations accomplish in four years or eight years - and we are just getting started” ; “The American Dream is surging - bigger and better than ever before. The American Dream is unstoppable, and our country is on the verge of a comeback the likes of which the world has never witnessed, and perhaps will never witness again.”

a905.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a905.speech: Hailed the achievements of his first six weeks, vowing to press on with his polarising bid to reshape the US government and end the Ukraine war - whatever the cost.

a905.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a905.speech: Had said on Monday that he would “let you know” during the speech about the fate of a minerals deal with Ukraine that remains unsigned after Zelensky’s disastrous visit.

a905.speaker: Karoline Leavitt, White House Press Secretary
a905.speech: Said the theme was the “renewal of the American dream and the renewal of the American dream is under way already”, telling Fox News.

a905.speaker: Karoline Leavitt, White House Press Secretary
a905.speech: “He’s going to dive into foreign policy, talk about his intention to end the war in Ukraine” ; said Trump would also discuss his “plan to bring all the hostages out of Gaza”.

a916.speaker: Azmi Balawneh, Director of Education in Tubas
a916.speech: Reported that the occupation forces moved into the village with bulldozers and began destroying the school, which was financed by the French agency ; added that the occupation had already ordered the school several months earlier to halt the works and had subsequently confiscated heavy bulldozers that were in use on the construction site.

a959.speaker: Zimbabwe Republic Police (statement)
a959.speech: According to a statement by the Zimbabwe Republic Police, the deceased have been identified as Joseph Myambo (45), Brighton Gwenzi Chibhosho (27), and Kudakwashe Marambire (44). The identity of the fourth victim is still pending, awaiting notification of next of kin.

a959.speaker: Local sources (anonymous)
a959.speech: According to local sources, the group believed that the aloe vera concoction would provide the desired effects associated with ‘guchu’.

a959.speaker: Witnesses
a959.speech: reported that the men had boiled the concoction in a bid to enhance their sexual performance, a practice that has gained popularity in some communities despite potential health risks.

a959.speaker: Dr Jonah Mashaba, Zimparks Eastern Region official
a959.speech: said aloes were a specially protected plant with over 500 species most of them common in Zimbabwe; he acknowledged that aloe has been used in the cosmetics and skin care industry, food and beverage industry as well for medicinal purposes but noted that not all species are safe for ingestion: “Aloes have been used since time immemorial as traditional medicine, for food and beverage, medicinal purposes for instance wound dressing and digestive issues. However, the only aloe which is medicinal is aloe vera and people may mistakenly identify aloe saponaria as aloe vera.” ; also highlighted that aloe globuligemma, nicknamed ‘witchdoctor’s aloe’ is a poisonous plant and is native to Southern Africa where it occurs in semi desert and dry bushland.

a959.speaker: Chief Zimunya, traditional leader
a959.speech: called for awareness campaigns and education of the public on the dangers of aloe; he acknowledged aloe as a plant traditionally used for various ailments, requesting more information on its adverse effects to be disseminated: “It is a pity that we lost several lives due to ignorance on the negative effects oif home-made concoctions. Aloe has always been known to have medicinal properties. It is my hope that an indepth investigation is instituted to the type of concoction that was prepared by these men and pin point the toxic element before we lose more lives.”

a959.speaker: Health experts
a959.speech: have consistently warned against the use of traditional concoctions without proper knowledge and guidance, particularly those that have not been scientifically validated for safety.

a1121.speaker: Nneka Acholonu Egbuna, USAID State2State Communication Specialist
a1121.speech: Said the workshop was to look into how information officers have been able to use the communication strategy adopted in the state since 2020 in discharging their duties ; Maintained that the Ebonyi State Communication Strategy was co-developed by government and stakeholders to improve communications between State Ministries, Departments and Agency officials and citizens for the purpose of strengthening state government responsiveness to the needs and priorities of its citizens.

a1121.speaker: Mrs. Ejiro Okotie, Gender and Social Inclusion Specialist with USAID State2State
a1121.speech: Highlighted on Understanding Gender and Social Inclusion Mainstreaming in Communication and implored the Information and Public Relations Officers to always promote positivism and empowering narratives technique in their reportage and charged them to avoid stereotype and bias reportage.

a1250.speaker: Owen Chataika, Mchinji District Health Office public relations officer
a1250.speech: “This year some new cases that have already been registered, which is something worrying” ; “For us to have already registered 11 new cases this year is worrisome. It shows that leprosy is still a hidden problem in our communities.”

a1250.speaker: Owen Chataika, Mchinji District Health Office public relations officer
a1250.speech: “As a way forward, the district health office plans to decentralise leprosy clinics and also lobby for more funds for mobile clinics, contact tracing and community sensitisation.”

a1250.speaker: Dickens Chimatiro, monitoring and evaluation officer for the National Tuberculosis and Leprosy Elimination Programme (Ntlep)
a1250.speech: “It is a cause for us to worry because even though we reached the elimination level in 1994, there are still some districts that are reporting more than one leprosy case per 10 000 people” ; “This means that we still have this burden in those districts. So it is a cause for worry, and that calls for concerted efforts to reduce the burden.” ; “Currently, Malawi has more than 600 people undergoing treatment for leprosy, and in terms of new cases, as of 2024, we have registered 367.”

a1250.speaker: World Health Organisation (WHO)
a1250.speech: According to the WHO, the disease is believed to be transmitted through droplets from the nose and mouth of an untreated case of leprosy, containing the causative agent, following prolonged, close contact; the disease does not spread through casual contact like shaking hands or hugging, sharing meals or sitting next to each other, and the patient stops transmitting the disease upon initiation of treatment.

a1250.speaker: Maziko Matemba, health issues commentator
a1250.speech: Believes that as a country, Malawi should ponder why there is resurgence of the disease after a very long time, and that as the country looks at what has gone wrong, there is need to also learn from what was done before in getting the elimination status of the condition ; “Factors contributing to the resurgence can be many. I think one thing that can be pointed out is surveillance and prevention, because normally when we say we have eliminated a disease, we also must have strong systems which can control the recurrence of the condition. What do we do? And also, how do we make sure that the disease does not come back? We have to check our systems to see what has gone wrong, though there can be many factors, including financing programmes for leprosy.”

a1256.speaker: Beijing / Chinese government
a1256.speech: Beijing says it has now curbed the spread of COVID-19, with domestic cases dwindling to zero Thursday.

a1256.speaker: Xi Jinping, Chinese President
a1256.speech: Pledged assistance to hardest-hit Italy and Spain in phone calls with their prime ministers, the official Xinhua news agency reported.

a1256.speaker: Xinhua news agency (official Chinese state agency)
a1256.speech: Reported that President Xi Jinping pledged assistance to hardest-hit Italy and Spain in phone calls with their prime ministers.

a1256.speaker: Xinhua news agency (official Chinese state agency)
a1256.speech: Xinhua said more aid and doctors from China would arrive in Serbia in the next few days.

a1256.speaker: Ursula von der Leyen, EU Commission President
a1256.speech: Said on Twitter this week that China would ship two million masks to Europe "immediately" and expressed her gratitude to Premier Li Keqiang. She said the EU helped China in January, by donating equipment, and tweeted: "Today, we're grateful for China's support."

a1256.speaker: Aleksandar Vucic, Serbian President
a1256.speech: "It has turned out that without you Europe can hardly defend itself," Vucic told Beijing's ambassador as Chinese virus tests arrived. ; He said the country had been waiting for its "Chinese brothers". ; The EU announced a ban on the export of medical equipment on Sunday, a move slammed by Vucic.

a1256.speaker: European Union (announcement)
a1256.speech: Announced a ban on the export of medical equipment on Sunday.

a1256.speaker: People's Daily (Chinese state-run newspaper, front-page commentary)
a1256.speech: A front-page commentary by the state-run People's Daily on Thursday emphasised China's role as a "responsible major country" that willingly cooperates with other nations.

a1256.speaker: Analysts (unnamed)
a1256.speech: Analysts say China is rushing to reposition itself as an alternative global leader.

a1256.speaker: Marina Rudyak, expert in Chinese foreign aid at the University of Heidelberg
a1256.speech: "Now, with the US government under Trump failing to provide any meaningful international response and the EU occupied with national responses, it offers China's government a unique opportunity to step into the empty spot," said Rudyak. ; Added that by doing so, China was also trying to rewrite the COVID-19 narrative, deflecting criticism of its initial attempts to cover up the outbreak and posing as the saviour of "other countries who either delayed their response or were less prepared than China."

a1256.speaker: Joerg Wuttke, president of the EU Chamber of Commerce in China
a1256.speech: "There are competing narratives evolving in Europe. Most people see China being responsible for this global crisis," said Wuttke. "But the generous humanitarian help from China will possibly swing the public opinion in Europe more in favour of China."

a1474.speaker: Judith-Ann Walker, Executive Director and founding member of the development Research and Projects Centre (dRPC)
a1474.speech: said that local intermediaries with a proven track record should be funded to cascade resources directly to grassroots NGOs. Speaking at the NGO Support Initiative (NSI) Grantees' Pause-and-Reflection Meeting, Ms Walker noted that this approach is more cost-effective and ensures funding reaches those closest to communities. "So we believe that local intermediaries, those that have proven themselves with a strong track record, not just the dRPC, there are many, that can be funded to cascade funding down, that is more cost effective, it is more efficient," she said ; stressed the importance of investing in governance, finance, and human resources over one-off projects, noting that past Gates Foundation and USAID programmes built organisations able to sustain impact.

a1474.speaker: Judith-Ann Walker, Executive Director of dRPC
a1474.speech: said the NSI is a support scheme that was conceived to assist Nigerian NGOs that lost USAID funding despite implementing high-impact work. She added that a second cohort is set to be launched next week, with a further 17 organisations expected to benefit.

a1474.speaker: Judith-Ann Walker, Executive Director of dRPC
a1474.speech: emphasised that collaboration with government agencies was a requirement for selection under the NSI and is crucial for sustainability, policy uptake and community acceptance. "There is a thinking of NGOs as a third sector, separate from the government, but we don't believe NGOs should be apart," she said. "For your work to be sustainable, to have impact and legitimacy, and to influence policy, you must collaborate."

a1474.speaker: PREMIUM TIMES (earlier report) / US State Department
a1474.speech: In February, PREMIUM TIMES reported that the US State Department announced a 92 per cent reduction in the USAID's foreign assistance budget, a move expected to drastically limit support for development efforts in countries such as Nigeria.

a1474.speaker: David Ahanor, Project Director of Rising Hope Girl's Foundation
a1474.speech: said his team used their NSI grant during the project's first phase to expand digital empowerment programmes and safe school awareness campaigns in marginalised communities of the Federal Capital Territory. Mr Ahanor said the team visited areas such as Kubwa, Bwari, and Chikakore, where digital infrastructure is almost non-existent. "With the NSI grant, we set up a digital lab in Dutse Alhaji, training over 200 students and equipping more than 100 teachers with skills in artificial intelligence and digital tools," he said ; recalling one memorable case, he spoke about a girl in Dutse Alhaji who had never used a computer before the project, whose first attempt at blogging and creating her own posts "opened a new world for her" and sparked visible excitement ; said the grant expanded his impact across Abuja and drew the attention of the Universal Basic Education Commission (UBEC), which expressed interest in a potential nationwide collaboration.

a1474.speaker: Oluwakemi Adenekan, Programme Manager at Headfort Foundation for Justice, Lagos State
a1474.speech: said a 25-member team, including 14 medical professionals, delivered mental health education, medical screenings, and on-the-spot treatment to 200 inmates [at the Female Correctional Centre, Kirikiri, Lagos], with many receiving healthcare for the first time since incarceration. Beneficiaries, she noted, included pregnant inmates, elderly women, and mothers with children.

a1576.speaker: Dr. Habtamu Itefa, Ethiopian Minister of Water and Energy
a1576.speech: Stated that Ethiopia's goal is to become an energy hub for the continent by connecting countries in the region with a reliable electricity supply, an ambition supported by the nation's rich natural resources, including water, wind, and solar ; Noted that power infrastructure projects currently underway will allow Ethiopia to export electricity to other countries, with efforts over the past five years already successfully increasing the national supply, and that projects like the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD) are key to accelerating these efforts and establishing Ethiopia's leadership in regional power connectivity.

a1767.speaker: US District Judge George O'Toole / federal judge in Massachusetts (court order)
a1767.speech: Ordered a temporary injunction on the plan's deadline — midnight Thursday — given by Musk for the country's more than two million government employees; the deadline is now extended to Monday, when Judge O'Toole will hold a hearing on the merits of the case brought by labor unions.

a1767.speaker: Karoline Leavitt, White House Press Secretary
a1767.speech: According to White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt, more than 40,000 staff have so far accepted the buyout deal.

a1767.speaker: Karoline Leavitt, White House Press Secretary
a1767.speech: Told reporters that federal workers should "accept the very generous offer" of a deferred resignation ; she said "competent" replacements would be found for those who "want to rip the American people off."

a1767.speaker: Union official (anonymous)
a1767.speech: A union official confirmed reports that the agency's global workforce would be slashed from over 10,000 to just under 300.

a1767.speaker: Randy Chester, vice president of the American Foreign Service Association
a1767.speech: "Eventually we will have to stop food distribution, because we won't have bodies in the field to make sure the food is actually being distributed," Randy Chester told reporters.

a1767.speaker: Robin Thurston, Democracy Forward
a1767.speech: Slammed the "unlawful seizure of this agency by the Trump-Vance administration, in a plain violation of basic constitutional principles about separation of power."

a1767.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a1767.speech: Has also repeatedly said he wants to shut down the Department of Education.

a1767.speaker: Official with the agency that manages government property (anonymous)
a1767.speech: Said the real estate portfolio, barring Department of Defense buildings, should be cut by "at least 50 percent."

a1767.speaker: Scott Bessent, US Treasury Secretary
a1767.speech: Told Bloomberg TV on Thursday that there was "a lot of misinformation" and that access to such data was only given to two Treasury employees who are working with Musk ; Bessent said those employees had "read-only" access, meaning they couldn't change the data.

a1767.speaker: The Wall Street Journal (report)
a1767.speech: Reported Thursday that one of those two resigned, after it emerged that he had advocated racism and eugenics on social media.

a1767.speaker: Elon Musk, head of the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE)
a1767.speech: Says the paid departures are a chance to "take the vacation you always wanted, or just watch movies and chill, while receiving your full government pay and benefits."

a1767.speaker: Unions (representing federal workers)
a1767.speech: Warn that without Congress signing off on the use of federally budgeted money, the agreements may be worthless.

a1767.speaker: Everett Kelley, president of the American Federation of Government Employees (AFGE)
a1767.speech: "Federal employees shouldn't be misled by slick talk from unelected billionaires and their lackeys."

a1767.speaker: Employee in the US Office of Personnel Management (anonymous)
a1767.speech: Said the plan was to encourage resignations through "panic": "We're trying to instill a panic so that people just walk out the door and leave government in a crippled state, which is partly their objective," the employee told AFP, speaking on condition of anonymity.

a1847.speaker: Maria Butina, Russian lawmaker for the ruling United Russia party
a1847.speech: Warned on Monday that the Biden administration's decision to allow Ukraine to use U.S.-made weapons to launch deep strikes into Russia could spark World War Three: "These guys, Biden's administration, is trying to escalate the situation to the maximum while they still have power and are still in office. ; I have a great hope that (Donald) Trump will overcome this decision if this has been made because they are seriously risking the start of World War Three which is not in anybody's interest. ; I guess there are some people in the United States who have nothing to lose for whatever reason or who are completely off the grid so much that they simply do not care."

a1847.speaker: Vladimir Putin, Russian President
a1847.speech: Has expressed strong concerns about Western involvement in the Ukraine conflict. On September 12, he stated that Western approval for Ukraine to use long-range missiles would directly draw NATO countries, the US, and European nations into the war, as NATO's military infrastructure and personnel would be necessary for targeting and firing the missiles ; in late October, he announced that Russia's defense ministry is exploring various response strategies if the US and its NATO allies assist Ukraine in launching deep strikes into Russian territory using Western-made long-range missiles.

a1847.speaker: NATO
a1847.speech: Has condemned Russia's actions in Ukraine, and its member states have imposed severe sanctions on Russia to starve its war machine of resources.

a1847.speaker: The Associated Press, citing one U.S. official and three people familiar with the matter
a1847.speech: Reported that the decision represents a significant shift in U.S. policy as Biden prepares to leave office.

a1847.speaker: Donald Trump, US President-elect
a1847.speech: Pledging to swiftly end the war and expressing scepticism about continued U.S. support.

a1925.speaker: Winnie Byanyima, UNAIDS executive director
a1925.speech: warned of a drastic rise in AIDS-related deaths and infections due to cuts in US foreign aid, potentially reversing 25 years of progress; said the sudden halt to US foreign aid funding has been "devastating" ; "It is reasonable for the United States to want to reduce its funding over time, but the sudden withdrawal of life-saving support is having a devastating impact," she told reporters in Geneva ; "We urge for a reconsideration and an urgent restoration of services, life-saving services."

a1925.speaker: Winnie Byanyima, UNAIDS executive director
a1925.speech: She warned that without more funding, "there will be an additional... 6.3 million AIDS-related deaths" in the next four years; at the last count, in 2023, some 600 000 AIDS-related deaths were registered globally, she pointed out: "So you're talking of a 10-fold increase." ; said her agency expected to see "an additional 8.7 million new infections" ; "You're talking of losing the gains that we have made over the last 25 years. It is very serious."

a1925.speaker: Winnie Byanyima, UNAIDS executive director
a1925.speech: "in the longer term, we see the AIDS pandemic resurging, and resurging globally" ; "Not just in the countries where now it has become concentrated, in low-income countries of Africa, but also growing amongst what we call key populations in Eastern Europe, in Latin America" ; "We will see a... real surge in this disease. We'll see it come back, and we'll see people die the way we saw them in the '90s and in the 2000s."

a1986.speaker: Dr. Abdullah Al Rabeeah, Advisor at the Royal Court and Supervisor General of KSrelief
a1986.speech: In his address during the conference, expressed heartfelt appreciation for the generosity shown by the donor community ; noted that these contributions not only demonstrate solidarity but also empower humanitarian organizations to deliver life-saving support, contributing to greater security and resilience for affected populations ; affirmed Saudi Arabia's ongoing commitment, through KSrelief, to expanding aid efforts in partnership with international stakeholders, ensuring that aid reaches those in urgent need.

a1986.speaker: Hissein Brahim Taha, OIC Secretary-General
a1986.speech: Stated that the conference is a testament to international unity, providing a platform for dialogue among humanitarian leaders and a foundation for coordinated, sustainable support for those affected by displacement ; "The presence of so many committed nations and organizations here today demonstrates a shared commitment to the values of solidarity and cooperation."

a1986.speaker: Antonio Guterres, United Nations Secretary-General
a1986.speech: Lauded Saudi Arabia and the OIC for leading the event, acknowledging the region's potential and the severe challenges it faces due to ongoing conflicts, climate disruptions, and economic strain; with over 30 million people in the Sahel and Lake Chad regions requiring immediate assistance, called for sustained humanitarian support and investment in long-term solutions, urging an end to hostilities, protection of civilians, and unhindered access for aid efforts.

a2024.speaker: Sahle-Work Zewde, President of Ethiopia
a2024.speech: Officially launched the "50 Million African Women Speak" Ethiopian platform and highlighted women's role in economic development and the importance of addressing structural barriers.

a2024.speaker: Filsan Abdullahi Ahmed, Minister of Women, Children & Youth
a2024.speech: "[It'll] allow women entrepreneurs to access crucial information and networking opportunities for their business," said Filsan, speaking during the event on the platform that was released as an app, "50MAWSP."

a2024.speaker: The Economist (Women's Economic Opportunity Index)
a2024.speech: Cited as a ranking measuring women's economic empowerment in which Ethiopia finds itself close to the bottom.

a2024.speaker: USAID
a2024.speech: According to USAID, women also face more limited access to credit and the market compared to men, and women's economic outcomes in rural areas are further complicated by a lack of infrastructure, health centres and schools.

a2134.speaker: Hamza Abdi Barre, Prime Minister of Somalia (official statement)
a2134.speech: Denied recent media reports suggesting that his government received aid money from Sweden in exchange for accepting the deportation of Somali migrants from Sweden; emphasized the historic and transparent nature of Somalia's relations with Sweden and clarified that Swedish aid to Somalia is not contingent upon any agreement to take back migrants and that all assistance is managed under strict oversight in compliance with international law. ; "All development assistance to Somalia is channeled through transparent mechanisms, including the World Bank, UN agencies, and the central government's financial system (Country System)."

a2134.speaker: Swedish media outlets (investigation)
a2134.speech: Revealed Sweden had allegedly provided $10 million in aid through the Somali Prime Minister's office, bypassing traditional aid agencies, and reported that this aid was part of a secret arrangement requiring Somalia to accept deported Somali migrants from Sweden.

a2467.speaker: Sam Matekane, Prime Minister of Lesotho
a2467.speech: Prime Minister Sam Matekane's mantra that the private sector should drive innovation and job creation.

a2467.speaker: Motlatsi Selele, LuCan's Deputy Laboratory Manager
a2467.speech: "We offer comprehensive quality control testing using globally recognized compendial methods that are rigorously verified by experienced scientists" ; "We are currently working towards achieving EUGMP certification. This will be another African first, and a game changer for our clients."

a2467.speaker: Motlatsi Selele, LuCan's Deputy Laboratory Manager
a2467.speech: "We are currently serving five local customers, including our sister company MG Health, which produces cannabis flower in Marakabei, a rural part of Maseru" ; "We carry out a variety of tests on cannabis products including cannabinoid profiles, terpenes, heavy metals, mycotoxins, residual solvents, water content, pesticides, thin-layer chromatography, and microbiological analysis. Cannabis is a very complex drug that must be handled delicately and in a controlled environment. As the only facility of its kind in the country, LuCan Labs is vital to the national regulatory framework, as it would be impossible to monitor the safety of cannabis medicines without proper testing. Our plan is to become the leading African testing facility—capable of testing all pharmaceutical products to ensure they are free from impurities and safe for consumption."

a2467.speaker: Motlatsi Selele, LuCan's Deputy Laboratory Manager
a2467.speech: "We currently have guests from the Medicines Control Authority of Zimbabwe (MCAZ) who are here to learn how we operate, so they can implement similar practices in their country, which also produces medical cannabis. Zambia has also shown interest in working with us—we will be helping them set up a similar facility."

a2467.speaker: Motlatsi Selele, LuCan's Deputy Laboratory Manager
a2467.speech: Mr Selele said his lab currently includes four expert scientists trained at the facility, and nine junior scientists—of which three recently completed their internships and six with two years of experience.

a2467.speaker: LuCan's four expert scientists (Mampoi Peete, Selometsi Baholo, Ntau Mafisa and Rethabile Nthebe)
a2467.speech: "Our duty is to analyse all samples that come into the lab—from cannabis flower to other matrices. We test their potency and evaluate the role each compound plays in medicinal efficacy, since most of the products we handle are used for pharmaceuticals. It is crucial that these products meet international quality standards. We test based on the standards set by the destination country. Most of our clients export to Europe, so we align our testing with the European Pharmacopoeia. We first develop analytical methods, then use state-of-the-art instruments and techniques to determine the content and purity of each product. LuCan has greatly supported Lesotho's cannabis market by enabling pre-sale product sampling for clients, ensuring compliance with quality controls and regulatory standards."

a2467.speaker: Douglas Mukena and Patience Mutsiba, representatives of the Medicines Control Authority of Zimbabwe (MCAZ)
a2467.speech: "We have been here since 8 June 2025 to launch an exchange programme between LuCan Labs and MCAZ. As Zimbabwe is one of the few countries that have legalised medical cannabis, we are here to learn cannabis analysis techniques and EU-GMP requirements. We are also establishing ties for study visits, proficiency testing, and collaborative analysis. We chose LuCan because it is the leading cannabis lab in the region. Since our arrival, we have already learned a lot that we can take back and implement. It will help Zimbabwe develop further and attract more investors. This marks the beginning of greater cooperation. We anticipate frequent exchanges, and eventually, we would like to see Zimbabwean scientists study here, and vice versa."

a2595.speaker: Jeffrey Sachs, economist (in his book “The End of Poverty: Economic Possibilities for Our Time”)
a2595.speech: Explains with sorrow that more than seven hundred million people in the world live in the pool of poverty, and that countries and the international community have not made sufficient efforts to eradicate poverty, which is produced and perpetuated by global systems.

a2595.speaker: Jeffrey Sachs, economist (in his book “The End of Poverty”)
a2595.speech: Demands systemic change in international financial institutions, because those who lead institutions such as the IMF and the World Bank favour rich countries, and trade laws, taxes and international relations are not friendly to third-world countries.

a2595.speaker: Jeffrey Sachs, economist (in his book “The End of Poverty”)
a2595.speech: Explains that the question of poverty is sensitive and advises that first we should understand poverty in its breadth, just as a doctor understands his patient — there is no single cure for the chronic disease of poverty; he gives the example of China, Singapore and India, which made great development strides through decisive leadership investing in technology, space, health, vocational skills, engineering and STEM (Human Capital Development), and advises that government invest in strategic sectors that directly touch people’s lives.

a2595.speaker: Jeffrey Sachs, economist (author, in his book “The End of Poverty”)
a2595.speech: Warns about discriminatory language and negative attitudes towards the poor as belittling and fuelling poverty, including institutions and politicians photographing the poor without their consent (“poverty porn”) and saying contemptuously “We must help these poor people” or “We do all this for the sake of the poor.”

a2595.speaker: Amartya Sen, philosopher and economist (in his book “Development as Freedom”)
a2595.speech: Says that poverty is not only that miserable state of lacking money and being unable to support oneself, but is a far deeper condition of being unable to use one’s freedom, gifts and God-given abilities.

a2595.speaker: Dambisa Moyo, economist from Zambia
a2595.speech: Says that we should gird ourselves and become self-reliant and abandon aid because it cripples us, as is seen in the USAID debacle.

a2595.speaker: Research/studies (unnamed)
a2595.speech: Show that income poverty among women is a great challenge that plunges them into gender-based violence and much abuse because of dependency, and that Tanzania’s economy has continued to grow statistically but with no real effect in reducing poverty, easing life or generating jobs and wages.

a2609.speaker: Ministry of Agriculture, Animal and Fisheries Resources of Burkina Faso
a2609.speech: Announced the temporary suspension of the issuing of import authorisations for broiler chicks.

a2647.speaker: World Bank health team support mission / delegation
a2647.speech: At the end of the mission, the delegation took stock of the results and the challenges. The mission noted that 83% of the targeted health facilities are enrolled in Results-Based Financing (RBF) as of the first quarter, and was able to observe that 24 Committees of Women Users of Health Services were created, 179 teachers trained in menstrual hygiene management and 231 people sensitised on the determinants of Gender-Based Violence in schools ; The mission also highlighted certain critical challenges, in particular the suspension of USAID, which has led to breaks in the supply of caesarean-section kits, family-planning commodities and blood-transfusion equipment.

a2647.speaker: Dr Ousmane Habib Diallo, national coordinator of ARISE/KENEYA YIRIWALI
a2647.speech: According to the national coordinator, the Results-Based Financing mechanism makes it possible to improve at once the quality of care, the optimal and efficient management of resources, and the promotion of a high-performing health system oriented towards quality and the values of accountability, transparency and social justice ; Said ARISE/KENEYA YIRIWALI is more than a project, it is an engine of transformation, an example of effective coordination between institutions, and a model of competitive governance: “The road is still long, but we will get there, gradually but surely. Because a strong health system is not decreed. It is built. Step by step. With and for those who are its reason for being.”

a2647.speaker: Dr Mahamadou Ibrahim Dicko, monitoring and evaluation officer
a2647.speech: Reassured: “A budget reallocation is under way to fill these critical gaps.”

a2647.speaker: Dr Moussa Yattara, Coordinator of the National Technical Unit for RBF
a2647.speech: Stated: “Our priority today is to make RBF an integrated function of the health system. This presupposes strong institutional ownership, adaptation to local realities and a clear commitment to sustainable financing.” Dr Yattara says he is optimistic about achieving this objective before September 2025.

a2721.speaker: International Monetary Fund (IMF)
a2721.speech: has urged Malawi and other African countries to strengthen their resilience to economic shocks beyond building financial buffers, as disruptions to global recovery persist.

a2721.speaker: International Monetary Fund (IMF), Regional Economic Outlook for sub-Saharan Africa
a2721.speech: observed that the region's economic recovery has been overtaken by recent shocks and growing macroeconomic imbalances; states that more than half of sub-Saharan African countries are facing varying economic imbalances, citing primary deficits below debt-stabilising levels, foreign reserves covering less than three months of imports, overvalued exchange rates, double-digit inflation, and high interest-to-revenue ratios exceeding 20 percent; revised the region's growth forecast downward to 3.8 percent in 2025 and 4.2 percent in 2026; attributes the slowdown to turbulent global conditions, including reduced external demand, falling commodity prices, and tightening financial markets. "Although market access improved in 2024, debt is still elevated for many countries, borrowing costs have increased, and global financial conditions are tightening."

a2721.speaker: International Monetary Fund (IMF)
a2721.speech: urged countries such as Malawi, Zimbabwe, the Republic of Congo, and Comoros to avoid accumulating payment arrears, which the IMF says "can only increase the cost of public service delivery and reduce the credibility of fiscal policy"; projects Malawi's economy to grow by 3.5 percent in 2025.

a2721.speaker: International Monetary Fund (IMF)
a2721.speech: downgraded its global growth projections to 2.8 percent for 2025 and 3 percent for 2026 - down from 3.3 percent projected in January 2025 - citing rising trade tensions and heightened policy uncertainty.

a2721.speaker: Betchani Tcheleni, Secretary to the Treasury
a2721.speech: said Malawi remains committed to its economic diversification and self-reliance agenda to reduce its vulnerability to both internal and external shocks; noted that while climate-related shocks have weighed heavily on Malawi's growth, a recovery is expected, driven by increased mining activity and diversification efforts. "We are expecting inflation to ease as food production has been relatively better this year compared to the past two years. There are also other efforts which are likely to significantly improve the balance of payments in the coming days, these will lower inflation and improve our macroeconomic environment."

a2721.speaker: Second-round crop estimates
a2721.speech: project maize production at 2.96 million metric tonnes - below the national requirement of 3.5 million metric tonnes.

a2721.speaker: Experts
a2721.speech: warn the maize deficit could keep food prices high.

a2721.speaker: Bertha Chikadza, President of the Economics Association of Malawi
a2721.speech: emphasized the need for deeper structural reforms. "In a dimming global outlook, Malawi's resilience will largely depend on sound fiscal management, strategic investment, and reforms that unlock domestic growth potential."

a2869.speaker: Ministry of Health of Tanzania
a2869.speech: Has said it has prepared five strategies that will help ensure that mental health challenges caused by various disasters such as conflicts, landslides and epidemics are addressed

a2869.speaker: Dr Grace Maghembe, Chief Medical Officer, Tanzania
a2869.speech: Making a statement in commemoration of World Mental Health Day, said the government has established psychological support desks, built the capacity of primary health care workers, collaborated with religious leaders, the media and social organizations in providing public education and combating stigma against those with mental health challenges. “Tanzania joins the World Health Organization (WHO) and its member states in celebrating World Mental Health Day. This year's theme is 'Access to Mental Health Services during Disasters and Emergencies' with a specific message to encourage mental health services and psychosocial support to be provided to all people, especially those affected by disasters such as floods, landslides, disease outbreaks, conflicts and road accidents”

a2869.speaker: Dr Grace Maghembe, Chief Medical Officer, Tanzania
a2869.speech: Said that according to WHO, in 2025 about a million people in the world will need humanitarian assistance due to conflicts, climate change and natural disasters, and noted that of them more than 300 million need mental health services and psychosocial support, which shows a significant increase in these important needs

a2869.speaker: World Health Organization (WHO) data cited
a2869.speech: According to WHO, in 2025 about a million people in the world will need humanitarian assistance due to conflicts, climate change and natural disasters

a2869.speaker: Dr Grace Maghembe, Chief Medical Officer, Tanzania
a2869.speech: Explained that in Tanzania psychological effects are clearly visible during various disasters such as the floods and landslides that occurred in Hanang, Manyara Region in 2023, where more than 5,600 people were directly affected. “In that event, the government in collaboration with stakeholders reached 3,380 people with psychological and social support, these services have also been provided in other disasters such as the COVID-19 outbreak, Mpox, Marburg and building collapses”

a2869.speaker: Dr Grace Maghembe, Chief Medical Officer, Tanzania
a2869.speech: Called on all Tanzanians to recognize that mental health services are a basic right of everyone, so help those facing these challenges by listening to them without judging them, encouraging them to seek help and participating in learning about mental health. “Let us build a society with compassion, hope, solidarity and love”

a2901.speaker: Dr. Abdiqani Sheikh Omar, former director general of the Ministry of Health and now a government advisor
a2901.speech: The U.S. Agency for International Development once provided 65% of Somalia's foreign aid, according to Dr. Abdiqani Sheikh Omar.

a2901.speaker: Save the Children
a2901.speech: Said the lives of 55,000 children will be at risk by June as it closes 121 nutrition centers it can no longer fund ; aid cuts mean that 11% more children are expected to be severely malnourished than in the previous year, Save the Children said.

a2901.speaker: Ahmed Moalin, former Somali Foreign Minister
a2901.speech: Told state-run TV last month that USAID had provided $1 billion in funding for Somalia in fiscal year 2023, with a similar amount expected for 2024.

a2901.speaker: U.S. State Department spokesperson (statement to the AP)
a2901.speech: Said “several lifesaving USAID humanitarian assistance programs are active in Somalia, including programs that provide food and nutrition assistance to children,” and they were working to make sure the programs continue when such aid transitions to the State Department on July 1.

a2901.speaker: Aid workers
a2901.speech: Say the problem is the U.S. hasn't made clear what programs are lifesaving, or whether whatever funding is left will continue after July 1.

a2901.speaker: CARE (aid group)
a2901.speech: Has warned that 4.6 million people in Somalia are projected to face severe hunger by June, an uptick of hundreds of thousands of people from forecasts before the aid cuts.

a2901.speaker: Ma'ow, bereaved father of Maka'il Mohamed (tailor)
a2901.speech: Said he had been unable recently to provide three meals a day for his family of six; his wife had no breast milk for Maka'il, whose malnutrition deteriorated between multiple trips to the hospital.

a2901.speaker: Doctors (Banadir Hospital)
a2901.speech: Confirmed that malnutrition was the primary factor in Maka'il's decline.

a2901.speaker: Simon Karanja, regional UNICEF official
a2901.speech: Said the funding cuts have left UNICEF's partners unable to provide lifesaving support, including therapeutic supplies and supplemental nutrition at a time when 15% of Somali children are acutely malnourished.

a2901.speaker: Abdullahi Hassan, Alight Africa worker
a2901.speech: Confirmed that the group had to close all their nutrition centers in several districts of Mogadishu.

a2901.speaker: Said Abdullahi Hassan, nutrition project supervisor for Alight Africa
a2901.speech: Said closures have caused, “tragically, the deaths of some children.”

a2901.speaker: Dr. Mohamed Jama, head of the nutrition center at Banadir Hospital
a2901.speech: According to Dr. Jama, more than 500 malnourished children were admitted to the center between April and May; he said such increases in patients usually occur during major crises like drought or famine but called the current situation unprecedented. “The funding gap has impacted not only the malnourished but also health staff, whose salaries have been cut,” he said.

a2901.speaker: Fadumo Ali Adawe, mother of five living in a displacement camp
a2901.speech: Said she urgently needed help for her 3-year-old daughter, malnourished now for nine months, and that the nearby nutrition center she frequented is now closed. “We are unsure of what to do next,” she said.

a2930.speaker: Saïd Nouh Hassan, Minister of the Interior of Djibouti (speech read by his technical adviser, Colonel Yahya Mohamed Magareh)
a2930.speech: Stressed from the outset that “Djibouti is determined to continue working for a world where every refugee is welcomed with dignity and respect”, before stating that “the Republic of Djibouti currently hosts on its territory 31,528 refugees and asylum seekers”, and launched an appeal to donors and the international community to increase financial support ; on refugees with disabilities: “we must redouble our efforts to guarantee that every refugee can live in dignity and above all attend to the specific needs of refugees with disabilities.”

a2930.speaker: Colonel Yahya Mohamed Magareh, technical adviser to the Ministry of the Interior and spokesman for the Minister
a2930.speech: Mentioned the enrolment of some 590 refugees with disabilities in the national system in order, he specified, to “allow them to access specific and adapted services”.

a2930.speaker: Yohondamkoul Sakor, UNHCR resident Representative in Djibouti
a2930.speech: Stressed the importance of solidarity and solutions for refugees, and recalled that, faced with the record increase in forcibly displaced people and persistent global conflicts, solidarity with refugees is more crucial than ever: “Refugees aspire to be given their chance, not to be given handouts. Many of them have skills, qualifications and innovative ideas. When they are given the opportunity, they make a real contribution to the community and to the economy of the host country.”

a2930.speaker: Fathia Alwan, director of the health and social development division of IGAD
a2930.speech: “The region is home to more than 23 million displaced people, including 5 million refugees” ; “despite a decrease in funds allocated to development and humanitarian aid”, the IGAD member states adopted “a regional approach for durable solutions following the summit of March 2017, focusing on local integration and regional cooperation” ; the IGAD Support Platform has enabled “notable advances, notably the inclusion of refugees in national education systems and the training of 755 teachers” ; reaffirmed IGAD’s continued commitment in favour of refugees and displaced people in the region.

a2930.speaker: José Barahona, United Nations system coordinator in Djibouti; Mohamed Ali Kamil, interim executive secretary of ONARS; and the representative of the ANPH
a2930.speech: Similar remarks were heard in their interventions.

a2965.speaker: Hans Essaadi, CEO of Nigerian Breweries
a2965.speech: Said in April 2023 that imports account for almost half of Nigerian Breweries’ input costs, leaving it at the mercy of exchange rate swings.

a2965.speaker: Nigerian Breweries (earnings release)
a2965.speech: “Foreign exchange volatility and limited access to foreign capital created additional hurdles for businesses, while the lingering effects of the fuel subsidy removal and Naira devaluation significantly increased operating costs across industries,” the company stated in its earnings release ; The consumer goods giant said it used the proceeds of its last year’s rights issue to “significantly reduce future currency risks.”

a2965.speaker: Nigerian Breweries (audited accounts issued on Friday)
a2965.speech: According to its audited accounts issued on Friday, sales improved by 80.8 per cent, taking revenue to a new milestone of N1.1 trillion, while the manufacturer posted N144.9 billion in net loss.

a2965.speaker: Heineken NV (financial report)
a2965.speech: “Net revenue (beia) was dampened by a negative translation impact of €1,656 million, or 5.5%, mainly due to the devaluation of the Nigerian Naira, and depreciation of the Brazilian Real and Mexican Peso,” the parent Heineken remarked in its own financial report issued on Wednesday ; Heineken acknowledged Nigeria as one of the markets that drove a 1.6 per cent increase in its beer volume globally last year.

a2994.speaker: Volker Türk, UN High Commissioner for Human Rights (statement)
a2994.speech: Argues in a statement that the plan, approved early today by Israel, "goes against the decision of the International Court of Justice that Israel must end its occupation as rapidly as possible, against the realisation of the agreed two-State solution and against the Palestinians' right to self-determination." ; Volker Türk believes that "this new escalation [in the Israeli-Palestinian conflict] will cause even more massive forced displacement, more deaths, more unbearable suffering, senseless destruction and atrocious crimes."

a2994.speaker: Volker Türk, UN High Commissioner for Human Rights
a2994.speech: The UN High Commissioner for Human Rights asks the Israeli government to allow humanitarian aid to enter the Gaza Strip "without obstacles", "instead of intensifying the war", in order to save civilian lives.

a2994.speaker: Volker Türk, UN High Commissioner for Human Rights
a2994.speech: The hostages, seized during the attack carried out on 7 October 2023 by Hamas on Israeli territory, "must be released immediately, and without demands, by the Palestinian armed groups", Volker Türk also demanded. ; "Palestinians arbitrarily detained by Israel must also be released immediately and without demands," the UN official added.

a2994.speaker: Health authorities in Gaza (records)
a2994.speech: Since then, more than 60,000 inhabitants of Gaza have died, almost half of them children and women, and more than 150,000 have been injured, according to the records of the health authorities, considered reliable by the UN.

a2994.speaker: Local authorities in Gaza (record released on Thursday)
a2994.speech: At least 198 of the deaths, including those of 96 children, occurred due to hunger and malnutrition, according to a record from the local authorities released on Thursday.

a2994.speaker: Two dozen UN experts, including Francesca Albanese, rapporteur for the Occupied Palestinian Territories (joint declaration, Geneva)
a2994.speech: Demanded on Thursday that Israel immediately restore unrestricted access for the organisation's humanitarian agencies to the Gaza Strip. The experts warned that more than 500,000 people, or a quarter of the population, are facing famine and 320,000 children under the age of 5 are at risk of acute malnutrition. ; "Starvation has been used as a savage weapon of war and constitutes a crime under international law," they said.

a2994.speaker: United Nations
a2994.speech: The UN has long declared the territory plunged into a grave humanitarian crisis, with more than 2.1 million people in a "catastrophic famine situation" and "the highest number of victims ever recorded" by the organisation in studies on world food security.

a2994.speaker: UN special commission
a2994.speech: At the end of last year, a UN special commission accused Israel of genocide in Gaza and of using hunger as a weapon of war.

a2994.speaker: Israeli Government
a2994.speech: The accusation was immediately refuted by the Israeli government, but without presenting any arguments.

a3023.speaker: Police report (report filed by the police)
a3023.speech: According to the report, it is alleged that the unknown driver of a white Toyota VVTi double cab with licence plate N126-092W (bearing a sticker – Donated by USAID) was driving from Nkurenkuru towards the direction of Rundu when he bumped the pedestrian who was attempting to cross the road.

a3023.speaker: Josephat Abel, Kavango West police commander
a3023.speech: “The driver overtook a vehicle, and it was in that process that the pedestrian was hit. The deceased was identified as Josephine Kasiku Haingura” ; “The driver is not known at this stage as he drove away after the accident, parked his vehicle at a nearby shebeen, locked the vehicle and fled on foot into the woods. Investigations into the incident continue.”

a3023.speaker: Namibian Police (Rundu)
a3023.speech: Have called on the public to identify the two victims, who have not yet been identified.

a3115.speaker: United Nations (UN)
a3115.speech: According to the UN, more than 25 million people in Sudan are currently facing imminent famine and require urgent humanitarian assistance.

a3115.speaker: UN experts (at the Human Rights Council, Geneva)
a3115.speech: Declared that "the deliberate targeting of humanitarian workers and local volunteers has undermined aid operations, putting millions of people at risk of famine." ; They added that "foreign governments providing financial and military support to both parties in this conflict are complicit in famine, crimes against humanity and war crimes."

a3115.speaker: Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), UNICEF and the World Food Programme (WFP)
a3115.speech: Have reported a rapid deterioration in living conditions, particularly for children: of the country's 24 million children, more than half, some 14 million, need urgent humanitarian assistance and most are out of school.

a3266.speaker: Amir Ali, US District Judge
a3266.speech: Ruled Wednesday that the administration's refusal to spend the aid likely violated a US law that governs how federal agencies make decisions; wrote that the administration has "given no justification to displace the bedrock expectation that Congress's appropriations must be followed," concluding that the defunding decisions violate the Administrative Procedure Act.

a3266.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a3266.speech: Asked Congress to claw back more than $4 billion in foreign aid set to expire this year, including $3.2 billion from the 2024 appropriations law covered by the latest ruling.

a3266.speaker: Bloomberg News
a3266.speech: Previously reported that Trump's move, known as a "pocket rescission," is timed to potentially allow him to avoid spending the money if Congress doesn't take action by the end of September and is widely seen as a test of his ability to use the manoeuvre to circumvent lawmakers' authority going forward.

a3266.speaker: The White House
a3266.speech: Didn't immediately respond outside regular business hours to an emailed request for comment.

a3269.speaker: Prince Lonkhokhela, Minister for Natural Resources and Energy of Eswatini
a3269.speech: Emphasised that while the country's mining potential is undeniable, its contribution to national development remains marginal: "More investors are entering the mining industry but the impact of the mining is yet to be realised as it remains in the extractive phase. Mineral processing is a pariah. It is so minimal, and this must change."

a3269.speaker: Prince Lonkhokhela, Minister for Natural Resources and Energy of Eswatini
a3269.speech: Challenged African leaders to ensure that mineral wealth drives industrialisation, energy access and job creation across the continent: "We believe that the benefits of Africa's mineral wealth must not only fuel industries abroad but must also power development at home: Creating jobs, expanding energy access and building inclusive prosperity." ; lamented the paradox of resource-rich African regions remaining impoverished despite decades of mining activity: "The AMSG should work tirelessly to change the status quo, which perpetuates poverty of mineral-rich areas, even after years of mining operations," noting that beneficiation and local processing were key to reversing this trend.

a3269.speaker: Central Statistical Office (latest data, 2024 GDP updates)
a3269.speech: Mining and quarrying contribute only 1.3 per cent to the country's gross domestic product; output for mining and quarrying activities fell sharply by 28.9 per cent in the first quarter of 2025, against 13.5 per cent growth in the previous quarter, driven primarily by the coal subsector, which suffered a 31.5 per cent year-on-year fall in output following weak demand from South Africa.

a3269.speaker: Economists
a3269.speech: Agree that Eswatini needs to diversify its mining sector beyond coal and invest in beneficiation to create value chains that support local industries.

a3430.speaker: Stakeholders at the Citizens' Budget Input Forum
a3430.speech: Have called on the government to prioritise sustainable financing for immunisation programmes to safeguard public health and drive economic growth; stressed the need for the government to increase domestic resource mobilisation and ensure timely disbursement of funds to meet the country's rising immunisation needs ; also urged the Ministry of Health to institutionalise a dedicated immunisation budget line in the national budget, with provisions for real-time tracking and monitoring to ensure transparency and efficiency.

a3430.speaker: Cecilia Senoo, Executive Director of Hope for Future Generations (HFFG)
a3430.speech: Emphasised the crucial role of individuals to act as the "voice of the voiceless" in ensuring equitable access to healthcare, particularly in the area of immunisation; stressed the need for all stakeholders within the healthcare system to come together and work collaboratively to sustain vaccine financing in Ghana; said collaboration among government agencies, development partners, and civil society was critical to maintaining effective immunisation programmes, adding that "The house must come together and work together to sustain vaccine financing" ; stressed the need to protect the future of children, adding that timely and consistent vaccination was essential for building a healthy and productive generation.

a3430.speaker: Sabina Morgan, Project Coordinator, HFFG
a3430.speech: Raised concerns about the inconsistency and delays in disbursing immunisation funds, stressing that such gaps threaten vaccine availability and the country's ability to respond swiftly during health emergencies ; "Timely and consistent financing for vaccines is not just a health imperative—it is a strategic investment that protects productivity and sustains economic growth."

a3430.speaker: Sabina Morgan, Project Coordinator, HFFG
a3430.speech: Said there was a need to develop a local vaccine production capacity to reduce dependence on external donors and ensure long-term sustainability of immunisation programmes; commended the establishment of a caucus in Parliament to institutionalise immunisation financing and strengthen accountability in fund utilisation.

a3430.speaker: Steven Atasige, Country Coordinator, Global Health Advocacy Incubator (GHAI)
a3430.speech: Called for stronger citizen engagement and sustainable financing strategies to secure the country's immunisation programmes in the 2026 national budget; said the forum was an opportunity for communities to have their priorities heard and reflected in the national budget ; "Our role is to help facilitate these discussions so the Ministry of Health and Ministry of Finance can incorporate these inputs into the 2026 budget."

a3430.speaker: Steven Atasige, Country Coordinator, Global Health Advocacy Incubator (GHAI)
a3430.speech: Commended the government for making significant strides to meet its vaccine financing obligations this year; said the country had already paid $24.6 million in co-financing for traditional vaccines before the end of the third quarter — a marked improvement from previous years when payments were often delayed ; "This is very encouraging. However, to sustain this progress, immunisation funding must be consistently prioritised in future budgets to prevent payment delays and avoid vaccine stockouts." ; stressed the importance of budget advocacy in ensuring consistent funding for public health interventions, particularly immunisation.

a3430.speaker: Kwaku Saffu-Mensah, Principal Planner, Ministry of Health (speaking on behalf of the Head of Planning and Budget)
